title: India's Sports Ministry Suspends Table Tennis Federation Over Governance Failures
excerpt: TTFI loses recognition as factional infighting, financial irregularities and Sports Code violations prompt government action against Indian table tennis body.
body:
• India's Sports Ministry has suspended the Table Tennis Federation of India's recognition as a National Sports Federation over persistent governance failures and violations of the National Sports Code.
  • The action follows months of factional infighting between TTFI President Meghna Ahlawat and suspended Secretary General Kamlesh Mehta, whose rival factions convened parallel meetings in January 2026.
  • A probe committee has flagged financial irregularities including unauthorized fund disbursement from the Sports Authority of India and conflicts of interest in commercial contracts.
  • The suspension comes less than four years after the Delhi High Court appointed an administrator to run TTFI following match-fixing allegations by star paddler Manika Batra.

India's Sports Ministry has suspended the Table Tennis Federation of India's (TTFI) recognition as a National Sports Federation (NSF), citing governance failures and non-compliance with the National Sports Development Code. The move strips the federation of government funding and official recognition until the issues are resolved.

The suspension marks the culmination of a turbulent period for Indian table tennis administration. TTFI has been embroiled in an increasingly acrimonious internal power struggle since elections in December 2022 brought Meghna Ahlawat, wife of former Haryana Deputy Chief Minister Dushyant Chautala, to the presidency and former India player Kamlesh Mehta to the secretary general's post.

Parallel Meetings and a Fractured Federation

The crisis escalated sharply in January 2026 when Mehta convened an Emergency Special General Meeting in Mumbai, attended by 12 state associations, where tournament dates and venues were announced. Ahlawat declared the meeting constitutionally invalid and called an Annual General Meeting in New Delhi on January 28, attended by 20 state associations. The AGM overturned Mehta's decisions and passed a resolution suspending him from the secretary's post with immediate effect.

Mehta has contested the action, alleging "a pattern of unilateral decision-making" by the president and claiming tenders were "not allotted through an open and fair process." He has said approaching the courts would be his "last resort" but that institutional safeguards had broken down.

"National sports federations function on public trust, public money and collective effort. Decisions affecting them must be taken carefully, transparently and strictly in accordance with established rules."

— Kamlesh Mehta, suspended TTFI Secretary General

Financial Irregularities Under Scrutiny

The TTFI executive committee has formed a three-member inquiry panel to investigate what it described as serious financial irregularities. Among the allegations: the unauthorized creation of "WTT India" without approval from the executive committee or AGM, irregular disbursement of funds received from the Sports Authority of India for the Vadodara WTT Feeder program, and distribution of sports kits over two years without mandatory approvals.

The federation also cited what it called a "clear conflict of interest" arising from Mehta's association with Eleven Sports Pvt. Ltd., the company behind Ultimate Table Tennis, India's franchise table tennis league. The current commercial agreement with Eleven Sports expires in August 2026, and the AGM resolved that TTFI should establish its own official league through a transparent bidding process.

A Pattern of Administrative Turmoil

Governance dysfunction is not new to Indian table tennis. In February 2022, the Delhi High Court suspended the TTFI after observing a "sorry state of affairs" in its functioning and appointed a Committee of Administrators (CoA) to oversee operations. The action followed match-fixing allegations by star paddler Manika Batra, who accused national coach Soumyadeep Roy of asking her to throw an Olympic qualifying match.

The Competition Commission of India also directed TTFI and its affiliates in 2024 to cease anti-competitive practices, finding that the federation had restricted the organization of independent tournaments and sought to prevent players from participating in unauthorized events.

The Sports Ministry had issued a show-cause notice to the TTFI in December 2025 for failing to prepare a full season calendar, including nationals across age groups. The Delhi High Court has separately urged the ministry to take firm action against NSFs that fail to comply with the Sports Code, observing that "twelve years is a long time to enable sports bodies to conform."

What Happens Next

With recognition suspended, TTFI loses access to government grants, the use of Sports Authority of India facilities, and the ability to field Indian teams in certain international events without special clearance. The International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF) will be monitoring the situation closely — it previously threatened to suspend TTFI membership in 2022 when court-appointed administrators were running the body.

The suspension adds table tennis to a growing list of Indian sports federations that have faced recognition crises. The Wrestling Federation of India's suspension was revoked earlier this year after 15 months, following its own governance overhaul. Indian table tennis officials will need to demonstrate compliance with the Sports Code to restore recognition — a process that could take months.
